1 OurBigBook.com
The extension K/F is a vector space over F. Since K is finite, a maximal linearly independent subset is finite and spans it; let its size be d. Relative to this basis, every element of K has a unique list of d coefficients in F. There are q choices for each coefficient, so
∣K∣=qd,d=[K:F].​
(1)
The inclusion F⊆K makes d≥1.

Words: 98 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 98
2 OurBigBook.com
Write Q=qm and take a splitting field L of XQ−X over F. Its formal derivative is −1, since the characteristic divides Q, so it has Q distinct roots in L. Let K be their set. The Frobenius endomorphism identity gives
(u+v)Q=uQ+vQ,(uv)Q=uQvQ.
(2)
Thus K contains 0,1 and is closed under addition, negatives and multiplication. If u=0 belongs to K, then (u−1)Q=(uQ)−1=u−1, so it is closed under inverses too. Hence K is a field with exactly Q elements. Every c∈F satisfies cq=c by Lagrange's theorem for finite groups applied to F×, together with the zero case; iterating gives cQ=c. Therefore
F⊆K,∣K∣=qm.​
(3)

3

Words: 50 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 50
3 OurBigBook.com
By the allowed finite multiplicative-subgroup theorem, the group K× is cyclic. Let z generate it. Every nonzero element of K is a power of z, hence belongs to F(z); zero belongs as well. Since the reverse inclusion is automatic,
K=F(z).​
(4)
Thus a finite extension of a finite field is a simple field extension.

For α=0, Lagrange's theorem for finite groups in K×, whose order is qm−1, gives αqm−1=1. The zero element satisfies the equation too, so every α∈K has αqm=α.
Now let f∈F[X] be irreducible of degree m. The quotient F[X]/(f) is a field with qm elements, by its basis 1,X,…,Xm−1. Its element X therefore satisfies Xqm−X=0. This means precisely that Xqm−X lies in the ideal (f), giving
f(X)∣Xqm−X.​
(5)

a OurBigBook.com
With N◃G, the internal semidirect product conditions are G=NH and N∩H={1}. Every element then has a unique expression nh. The extra data needed to reconstruct the group are the conjugation action
ϕ:H→Aut(N),ϕh​(n)=hnh−1.
(6)
On the set N×H, the external semidirect product N⋊ϕ​H has multiplication
(n,h)(n′,h′)=(nϕh​(n′),hh′).​
(7)
The map (n,h)↦nh identifies it with G. A direct product results when this action is trivial.
For example, S3​=A3​⋊⟨(12)⟩≅C3​⋊C2​. The two subgroups intersect trivially and their orders multiply to six, so they generate S3​. Conjugation by the transposition inverts the three-cycle. This action is nontrivial, and S3​ is nonabelian whereas C3​×C2​ is abelian, so this is not their direct product.

b

Words: 70 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 70
b OurBigBook.com
Use composition from right to left. Applying (C,d) and then (A,b) gives
v↦A(Cv+d)+b=ACv+(Ad+b),
(8)
so
(A,b)(C,d)=(AC,Ad+b).​
(9)
The product remains an affine transformation because AC is invertible. Composition of functions is associative. The identity is (I,0), and solving w=Av+b gives the inverse
(A,b)−1=(A−1,−A−1b).​
(10)
Thus these transformations form the affine group. The representation by (A,b) is unique: evaluating at zero determines b, and then evaluating on the standard basis determines A.

c OurBigBook.com
Embed GLn​(F) by A↦(A,0). The multiplication and inverse formulas show that this is an injective group homomorphism, so its image H is a subgroup. The translations form N={(I,c):c∈Fn}, with (I,c)(I,d)=(I,c+d) and inverse (I,−c). Hence N is isomorphic to the additive group of Fn.
For an arbitrary affine transformation,
(A,b)(I,c)(A,b)−1=(I,Ac).​
(11)
Conjugation therefore preserves N, proving that N is normal in G.

Every affine transformation factors as
(A,b)=(I,b)(A,0),
(12)
so G=NH. A translation fixing zero has zero translation vector, so H∩N={(I,0)}. Together with normality from part (c), these are the internal semidirect product conditions. Thus
G≅(Fn,+)⋊GLn​(F).​
(13)
The reconstruction data are the additive group Fn, the linear group GLn​(F), and its standard action A:c↦Ac on translations. In pair notation (b,A), the product is (b,A)(d,C)=(b+Ad,AC), equivalent to the formula in part (b).

i OurBigBook.com
A primitive root modulo p is a residue class generating the cyclic multiplicative group (Z/pZ)×, so its order is p−1. If g is one generator, all generators are gj with gcd(j,p−1)=1. Thus the number is
φ(p−1),​
(15)
where φ is Euler's totient function. This includes p=2, with φ(1)=1.

For n≥1, the zero residue contributes zero. Write S=∑x∈Fp×​​xn. Multiplication by any nonzero α permutes these residues, so S=αnS in Fp​. If (p−1)∤n, choose a primitive root g; then gn=1, and (1−gn)S=0 forces S=0.
If (p−1)∣n, every nonzero x has xn=1, so S=p−1≡−1(modp). Therefore
x=1∑p​xn≡{0,−1,​(p−1)∤n,(p−1)∣n​(modp)(n≥1).​
(16)
The source also lists n=0, although its premise assumes n≥1. For that separate case, the integer sum has p terms each equal to one, so it is zero modulo p.

iii OurBigBook.com
The Legendre symbol equal to 1 says that a is a nonzero square modulo p. Choose one root r=0. Then −r is another root, distinct because p is odd. Any solution x satisfies
0=x2−r2=(x−r)(x+r)
(17)
in the field Fp​, so x=r or x=−r. Thus there are
2 solutions.​
(18)

iv

Words: 73 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 73
iv OurBigBook.com
Let R be the sum of the nonzero quadratic residues. Each has two square roots by part (iii), so
2R≡∑x=1p−1​x2≡0(modp),
(19)
where part (ii) applies because p>3 makes p−1 not divide 2. Since 2 is invertible modulo p, R≡0.
The sum of all nonzero classes is p(p−1)/2≡0(modp). Subtracting R shows that the sum of quadratic nonresidues is also zero. Consequently both requested sums vanish modulo p.

Part (ii), with exponent 30, shows that a prime q fails to divide the sum precisely when q−1 divides 30. The positive divisors are 1,2,3,5,6,10,15,30. Adding one gives 2,3,4,6,7,11,16,31, of which the primes are
q∈{2,3,7,11,31}.​
(20)
For these primes the sum is −1 modulo q; for every other prime it is zero.

The monotone convergence theorem states that for nonnegative measurable functions fn​↑f almost everywhere, ∫f=limn​∫fn​, allowing the value +∞.
The dominated convergence theorem states that if measurable functions fn​→f almost everywhere and ∣fn​∣≤g almost everywhere for some integrable g, then f is integrable and ∫fn​→∫f. In fact ∫∣fn​−f∣→0 as well. Both statements apply on any measure space.

1 OurBigBook.com
Apply the monotone convergence theorem to sN​=∑k=1N​∣ak​∣. Its limit s satisfies
∫s=∑k=1∞​∫∣ak​∣<∞.
(21)
Thus s is finite almost everywhere, which proves absolute convergence of ∑k​ak​ almost everywhere. Define its sum a there, and set a=0 on the exceptional null set. Then ∣a∣≤s, so a is integrable. The partial sums of ∑k​ak​ are also dominated by s; dominated convergence gives
∫k=1∑∞​ak​=N→∞lim​k=1∑N​∫ak​=k=1∑∞​∫ak​.​
(22)
The series of integrals converges absolutely, since ∣∫ak​∣≤∫∣ak​∣.

For 0<x<1, expand (1−x)−2=∑k≥1​kxk−1. Multiplying by (logx)2 gives nonnegative terms, so the monotone convergence theorem permits termwise integration. Put x=e−t to obtain
∫01​xk−1(logx)2dx=∫0∞​t2e−ktdt=k32​,
(23)
where scaling followed by two integrations by parts evaluates the last integral. Hence
∫01​(1−xlogx​)2dx=2k=1∑∞​k21​=3π2​.​
(24)
The finite value also establishes integrability at both endpoints.

D4 OurBigBook.com
A sufficient differentiation under the integral sign theorem is the following local domination criterion. Suppose u(t,⋅) is measurable for each t, u(t0​,⋅) is integrable at one point of a neighborhood J of t0​, and for almost every x the function u(⋅,x) is differentiable on J. Assume an integrable function gJ​ satisfies ∣∂t​u(t,x)∣≤gJ​(x) for t∈J and almost every x. Then I is differentiable on the interior of J and
I′(t)=∫E​∂t​u(t,x)dx.​
(25)
The mean value theorem bounds the difference quotients by gJ​, and the dominated convergence theorem passes their pointwise limit through the integral. Applying this criterion locally throughout (a,b) proves differentiability there. One may impose the stronger condition that every u(t,⋅) is integrable from the outset.

For every integer j≥0, the jth derivative with respect to t of cos(tcosx) is (cosx)j times a sine or cosine with a sign. Its absolute value is at most 1 on the finite interval [0,π/2]. This is an integrable dominating function independent of t. Repeated differentiation under the integral sign is therefore justified for every order, giving J0​∈C∞(R).

Now integrate the derivative
dxd​(sinxsin(tcosx))=cosxsin(tcosx)−tsin2xcos(tcosx).

K(t)=t∫t∞​s2coss​ds.

dtd​∫t∞​s2coss​ds=−t2cost​.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
A subset A is connected if its subspace topology admits no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets. Equivalently, every continuous map A→{0,1}, with the target discrete, is constant: a nonconstant map gives the separation by its two fibers, and a separation defines such a map.
ii
Words: 47 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 47
ii OurBigBook.com
The connected subsets of the usual real line are the empty set and all intervals, including singletons, bounded intervals of any endpoint type, rays, and the whole line. Equivalently, a nonempty subset is connected exactly when it contains every point between any two of its points.

Solution
Words: 66
iii OurBigBook.com
Use the characterization by continuous maps to the discrete two-point space. Let A=⋃i​Ai​ and let f:A→{0,1} be continuous. Its restriction to each connected Ai​ is constant. Since Ai​∩Aj​=∅, those two constants agree for every pair i,j. Hence f is constant on their union. Thus the union is connected. If the indexing set is empty, the union is empty and is connected directly.

Ka​=⋃{S⊆X:S is connected and a∈S}.​
(32)
This family is nonempty because it contains {a}. All its members intersect at a, so part (a)(iii) proves that Ka​ is connected. It contains a and, by its construction, contains every connected subset containing a. Thus it has exactly the required largest-subset property. This is the connected component containing a.

Suppose two components K and L intersect. Their union is connected by part (a)(iii). It contains the point used to define K, so maximality forces K∪L⊆K, giving L⊆K. The same reasoning with L gives K⊆L. Hence K=L. Thus distinct connected components are disjoint.

Words: 75 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 75
iii OurBigBook.com
Let C be a component of the open set X⊆R. Being a connected subset of the real line, C is an interval. For any x∈C, openness of X gives ϵ>0 with (x−ϵ,x+ϵ)⊆X. This interval is connected and meets C, so their union is connected. Maximality of C makes the entire interval lie in C. Thus every point of C is interior, so each component is an open interval, allowing unbounded endpoints.

Words: 81
iv OurBigBook.com
Every point belongs to its component, so the components cover X; by part (ii) they are pairwise disjoint, and by part (iii) they are nonempty open intervals. Each contains a rational number. Fix an enumeration of Q and choose the first rational belonging to each component. Distinct components receive distinct rationals, giving an injection from the component family into a countable set. Therefore
X is a countable union of pairwise disjoint open intervals.​
(33)
The empty open set is represented by the empty union.

A subset K of a topological space is compact if every cover of K by open subsets of the ambient space has a finite subcover. This is equivalent to compactness of K with its subspace topology.

ii OurBigBook.com
A subset B of a metric space is bounded if it lies in some ball of finite radius: there are x0​ in the space and R<∞ with d(x,x0​)≤R for every x∈B. For a nonempty subset, this is equivalent to finite diameter, supx,y∈B​d(x,y)<∞. The empty subset is bounded by convention.
iii
Words: 240 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 240
iii OurBigBook.com
In an arbitrary topological space, compact need not imply closed. In a two-point indiscrete space, a singleton is compact but not closed. Closed need not imply compact either: R is closed in itself but the cover {(−n,n):n≥1} has no finite subcover. One general theorem that does hold is that a closed subset F of a compact space K is compact: adjoin K∖F to any relative open cover of F, take a finite cover of K, and discard that additional set.
In a Hausdorff space, every compact subset K is closed. For y∈/K, separate y from each x∈K by disjoint open sets Vx​ about y and Ux​ about x. Finitely many Ux​ cover K; the intersection of their corresponding Vx​ is a neighborhood of y disjoint from K. Thus the complement of K is open. The converse still fails, as the real-line example shows.
In every metric space, compact subsets are bounded. Cover a nonempty K by unit balls centered on K and take a finite subcover; the triangle inequality bounds all points relative to any one of the finitely many centers. The converse fails even for closed bounded subsets of general metric spaces. An infinite set with discrete metric d(x,y)=1 for distinct points is closed and bounded in itself, but its cover by singleton balls has no finite subcover. Thus compact implies closed and bounded in a metric space, while closed and bounded need not imply compact.

Words: 50
iv OurBigBook.com
By the Heine-Borel theorem, a subset of R is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. Consequently the compact intervals are
[u,v]with finite u≤v,​
(34)
including singleton intervals. The empty interval is compact too, if included in the interval convention. Nonempty open, proper half-open, and unbounded intervals are not compact.
v
Words: 140 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 140
v OurBigBook.com
For any topological target Y, f(K) is compact. Pull an open cover of f(K) back by f, take a finite subcover of K, and map the covering statement forward. Without a separation assumption on Y, the image need not be closed, as a constant map into a nonclosed singleton of an indiscrete space shows.
If Y is a metric space, f(K) is also closed in Y, bounded, totally bounded, complete with its inherited metric, and sequentially compact. Closedness uses the Hausdorff theorem from part (iii); total boundedness follows by taking finite subcovers of the covers by balls of any fixed radius. Compact metric spaces are sequentially compact, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit, proving completeness. These properties are asserted for the image subset, without requiring the whole ambient metric space to be complete.

A C1 embedded submanifold M⊆Rn of dimension n−1 is locally the graph of a C1 function of n−1 coordinates after a change of coordinates. Equivalently, near each point x0​∈M it is a regular level set {x:h(x)=0} of a C1 scalar function with ∇h(x0​)=0.
The Lagrange multiplier theorem says that if a C1 function F has a constrained local extremum at x0​ on such a level set, then
∇F(x0​)=λ∇h(x0​)​
(42)
for some real λ. Indeed the derivative of F must vanish on the tangent space Tx0​​M=kerDh(x0​), whose normal space is the line spanned by ∇h(x0​). The nonzero-gradient condition is essential.

At a regular constrained extremal, the first variations satisfy δI=λδJ for a constant Lagrange multiplier λ. One way to justify this is to choose a variation for which δJ=0, use it to correct any other variation to preserve the constraint by the implicit function theorem, and differentiate I along that corrected family. This gives the same ratio λ for all variations. The exceptional case δJ=0 for every variation requires the usual separate abnormal-extremal analysis.
Set L=F−λG. Integration by parts in its first variation gives
δ(I−λJ)=[Ly′​η]ab​+∫ab​(Ly​−dxd​Ly′​)ηdx.
(48)
Taking compactly supported variations and applying the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations yields the Euler-Lagrange equation. For the quadratic integrands, it is
(py′)′+(q+λr)y=0,​
(49)
or Ly=λry with Ly=−(py′)′−qy. If endpoint values are free, independent endpoint variations give the natural conditions
p(a)y′(a)=p(b)y′(b)=0.​
(50)
At a prescribed endpoint the variation instead vanishes and no natural condition is added there.
Under these natural conditions, integration by parts gives
2I=∫ab​(py′2−qy2)dx=[py′y]ab​+∫ab​yLydx=λ∫ab​ry2dx=2λJ.
(51)
Hence I=λJ​. For two solutions satisfying the same natural conditions, subtract their cross-multiplied equations and integrate:
(λm​−λn​)∫ab​rym​yn​dx=∫ab​(yn​Lym​−ym​Lyn​)dx=0.
(52)
The final equality is the vanishing endpoint boundary form. Thus distinct eigenvalues give
∫ab​rym​yn​dx=0.​
(53)
The same argument works for other common homogeneous boundary conditions making that boundary form zero.
In the Legendre case, ((1−x2)yn′​)′+λn​yn​=0. Comparing coefficients of xn in a degree-n solution gives λn​=n(n+1), so different degrees have different eigenvalues. A degree-zero solution is y0​=C0​. A linear solution Ax+B must be orthogonal to the nonzero constant solution, so B=0 and y1​=C1​x. Write y2​=Ax2+Bx+C. Orthogonality to x gives B=0, and orthogonality to 1 gives 2A/3+2C=0. Therefore
y2​=C2​23x2−1​.​
(54)
The constants are free normalization factors; for solutions of the stated exact degrees they are nonzero. The natural endpoint conditions hold automatically for these polynomials because p(±1)=0.

For −V0​<E<0, set k=2m(V0​+E)​/ℏ>0 and κ=−2mE​/ℏ>0. Oddness removes the interior cosine solution, and normalizability removes the growing exponentials outside. A continuous odd candidate can therefore be written
ψ(x)=A⎩⎨⎧​−sin(ka)eκ(x+a),sin(kx),sin(ka)e−κ(x−a),​x≤−a,∣x∣<a,x≥a.​

η=−ξcotξ,ξ2+η2=ℏ22mV0​a2​.​

Physical bound states require ξ,η>0. On 0<ξ<π/2, the cotangent condition gives negative η, so no physical intersection occurs. On (π/2,π), the curve −ξcotξ rises from zero to positive infinity, while the positive quadrant of the circle decreases. Their first intersection exists exactly when the circle radius R=2mV0​a2/ℏ2​ exceeds π/2.

The Milne-Thomson circle theorem says that if a complex potential f(z) has no singularities on or inside ∣z∣=a, then a circular impermeable boundary can be introduced by taking
W(z)=f(z)+f∗(a2/z),f∗(w)=f(w)​.
(59)
The new singularities are the reflected ones inside the circle. On ∣z∣=a, a2/z=z, so W(z)=f(z)+f(z)​ is real; the stream function is constant and there is no normal velocity. At infinity the added term tends to f∗(0), a harmless potential constant, so it preserves the far-field flow. This proves the theorem with zero added net circulation about the cylinder. A logarithmic term may then specify a different cylinder circulation.
For f(z)=−iΓlog(z−b)/(2π), put c=a2/b. The reflected term is
f∗(a2/z)=2πiΓ​log(a2/z−b)=2πiΓ​log(z−c)−2πiΓ​logz+constant,
(60)
with locally consistent logarithm branches. The circle-theorem solution has zero cylinder circulation: its image vortex at c and its central vortex cancel. To impose circulation −Γ, add iΓlogz/(2π). The result is
w(z)=−2πiΓ​log(z−b)+2πiΓ​log(z−c)+constant.​
(61)
It consists of the physical vortex and an opposite image vortex inside the obstacle. On the circle, ∣z−b∣=(b/a)∣z−c∣, so its stream function is indeed constant.
The complex velocity is
q(z)=w′(z)=−2πiΓ​(z−b1​−z−c1​).
(62)
Inside the positively oriented obstacle contour, q2 has only the double pole at c. Its residue is
Resz=c​q(z)2=dzd​[−4π2(z−b)2Γ2(b−c)2​]​z=c​=−2π2(b−c)Γ2​.
(63)
The residue theorem and the supplied Blasius force theorem therefore give
Fx​−iFy​=2iρ​(2πi)[−2π2(b−c)Γ2​]=2π(b−c)ρΓ2​.
(64)
Consequently
Fx​=2π(b2−a2)ρΓ2b​,Fy​=0.​
(65)
The force points toward the held vortex, independent of the sign of its circulation.
The residue calculation is the force on a circular cylinder from a held exterior vortex.

The significance level of a test is a bound α on its probability of rejecting a true null; for a composite null the bound is uniform over its parameter values. Its power at an alternative parameter is its rejection probability under that parameter.
The Neyman-Pearson lemma concerns a simple null density f0​ and a simple alternative density f1​ for the whole sample. Among tests of size at most α, a most powerful test rejects where f1​>kf0​, accepts where f1​<kf0​, and if necessary randomizes on equality so that its size is α. Let its rejection probability function be ϕ∗​, with 0≤ϕ∗​≤1, and let ϕ be any competing test of size at most α.
Pointwise,
(ϕ∗​−ϕ)(f1​−kf0​)≥0:
(99)
on the rejection side both factors are nonnegative, and on the acceptance side both are nonpositive. Integrating gives
∫ϕ∗​f1​−∫ϕf1​≥k(∫ϕ∗​f0​−∫ϕf0​)≥0.
(100)
Thus the likelihood-ratio test has at least as much power as any competitor. Even when the sample has a continuous density, the likelihood ratio can have an atom, so boundary randomization may still be necessary in the general statement. For the exponential test below the statistic has a continuous distribution and no randomization is needed.

Under a true alternative λ, S∼Gamma(n,λ), so its attained power is
Q(λ)=1−F(q(1−α;n,λ0​);n,λ).​
(103)
For each λ<λ0​, the Neyman-Pearson lemma bounds the power of every other level-α test by this value. Hence the displayed function is not only an upper bound but the attainable power envelope on the specified alternative.

A best approximation to x from Un​ is a vector u∗​∈Un​ such that
∥x−u∗​∥=u∈Un​inf​∥x−u∥.​
(104)
The definition requires attainment of the infimum. This finite-dimensional subspace does have such an approximation, as the explicit projection below shows; completeness of the whole inner-product space is unnecessary.

b OurBigBook.com
Expand both squared norms using the inner product:
∥x±y∥2=∥x∥2+∥y∥2±2Re⟨x,y⟩.
(105)
Adding cancels the cross terms, giving the parallelogram law
∥x−y∥2+∥x+y∥2=2(∥x∥2+∥y∥2).​
(106)
The real part may be omitted in a real inner-product space.

Suppose u,v∈Un​ both minimize the distance, with common value d. Apply the parallelogram identity to x−u and x−v:
4​x−2u+v​​2+∥u−v∥2=4d2.
(107)
The midpoint belongs to the linear subspace Un​, so its distance from x is at least d. It follows that ∥u−v∥2≤0, hence u=v. Thus the best approximation is unique.

⟨x−v,ej​⟩=⟨x,ej​⟩−∑k​⟨x,ek​⟩⟨ek​,ej​⟩=0
(108)
for every j. Hence x−v is orthogonal to Un​. For any u∈Un​, the Pythagorean identity gives ∥x−u∥2=∥x−v∥2+∥v−u∥2, so v is the unique best approximation. Therefore
Pn​x=k=1∑n​⟨x,ek​⟩ek​.​

a OurBigBook.com
Assume the usual nondegenerate interval a<b. The integral is bilinear and symmetric because the functions and weight are real. It is nonnegative on (f,f). If f is nonzero at a point, continuity makes ∣f∣ bounded below by a positive number on a nontrivial relative interval nearby, and the positive continuous weight is also bounded below there. Hence ∫ab​f2w>0. Thus the formula is positive definite and defines an inner product.
The functions are orthogonal precisely when
⟨f,g⟩=∫ab​f(x)g(x)w(x)dx=0.​
(112)
A singleton interval would make this integral zero for every function, so the condition a<b is necessary.

b

Words: 192 Articles: 1
P4 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 192
b OurBigBook.com
The intended orthogonal-polynomial convention is degpk​=k. An arbitrary orthonormal basis without this degree ordering does not satisfy the claim: permuting a standard basis can place the nonzero constant polynomial last, where it has no roots rather than n+1. The following proof uses the required degree ordering.
It makes pk​ orthogonal to every polynomial of degree less than k, since p0​,…,pk−1​ form a basis of that lower-degree space. Let c1​,…,cr​ be the distinct roots in (a,b) at which pk​ changes sign, and put q(x)=∏j=1r​(x−cj​), with q=1 if r=0. The product pk​q has constant sign on (a,b) except at its finitely many zeros: each sign change of pk​ is canceled by that of q.
If r<k, then q has degree below k, so orthogonality gives ∫ab​pk​qw=0. But a nonzero constant-sign continuous product against the positive weight has a nonzero integral, a contradiction. Thus r≥k. Since degpk​=k, there are exactly k such roots, all simple, with no additional endpoint roots. In particular
pk​ has exactly k distinct roots, all in (a,b).​
(113)
This also includes k=0, where the polynomial is nonzero constant and has no roots.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
Use the intended degree ordering from part (b). Let ℓj​ be the degree-n Lagrange cardinal polynomial at the distinct roots x0​,…,xn​ of pn+1​:
ℓj​(x)=∏i=j​xj​−xi​x−xi​​,wj​=∫ab​ℓj​(x)w(x)dx.
(114)
For any f∈Π2n+1​, polynomial division gives f=spn+1​+r with degs≤n and degr≤n. Orthogonality of pn+1​ to Πn​ makes the integral of spn+1​ zero, and that product also vanishes at every quadrature node. Meanwhile r=∑j​r(xj​)ℓj​ by interpolation. Consequently
∫ab​f(x)w(x)dx=∫ab​r(x)w(x)dx=j=0∑n​wj​f(xj​).​
(115)
Thus the rule is exact up to degree 2n+1. To determine the sign of a weight, apply exactness to ℓj2​, of degree 2n:
wj​=i∑​wi​ℓj​(xi​)2=∫ab​ℓj​(x)2w(x)dx>0.​
(116)
The inequality is strict because ℓj​ is a nonzero polynomial and the weight is positive. This is the Gaussian quadrature construction; the source asks only for nonnegative weights, and the proof gives positivity.
